entries.title: Bomberman

entries.why_it_matters: Began the Bomberman series. Hudson claimed nearly one million copies sold by 1989, and director Shinichi Nakamoto considered this console version definitive.

entries.title: A Boy and His Blob: Trouble on Blobolonia

entries.why_it_matters: Won 'Best of Show' at CES 1989 and a Parents' Choice Award. GamesRadar noted it as an early landmark for an AI-controlled companion.
entries.gameplay_notes: The boy can't jump or swim and dies from long falls. Feed Blobert flavoured jelly beans to turn him into tools (licorice for a ladder, apple for a jack, and so on) and whistle to call him back. Collect treasure to buy vitamins for the VitaBlaster used on Blobolonia.

difficulty.reason: Trial-and-error jelly-bean puzzles with limited supplies.

entries.title: Bubble Bobble

entries.why_it_matters: One of Taito's biggest hits and often listed among the greatest games. It inspired many screen-clearing platformers, was one of the first games with multiple endings, and is on the NES Classic Edition.
entries.gameplay_notes: Blow bubbles to trap enemies, then pop them for food bonuses; pop several at once for bigger rewards. Ride bubbles to reach high areas. entries.title: Contra
entries.summary: Konami's in-house NES version of its 1987 arcade run-and-gun. Commandos Bill and Lance fight through eight stages against the alien-backed Red Falcon.
entries.why_it_matters: EGM's Best Action Game of 1988. It made the Konami Code famous and launched Contra as a flagship home series.
entries.gameplay_notes: Side-view stages plus pseudo-3D base stages played into the screen. The NES version recomposes the arcade's seven stages into eight, with new Snowfield, Energy Zone, Hangar and Alien Lair stages. Up to two players simultaneously.

difficulty.reason: Widely considered difficult; the Konami Code's 30 lives (instead of three) became famous as the way to finish it.

entries.title: Crystalis

entries.title: Deadly Towers
entries.summary: Irem-commissioned action RPG (developed by Lenar and Tamtex, published in NA by Broderbund). Prince Myer must burn seven magic bells in a sacred flame and defeat Rubas, the Devil of Darkness.
entries.why_it_matters: Along with Rygar, among the first Japanese action RPGs published in NA, and Broderbund's best-selling first-wave NES title.
entries.gameplay_notes: Nonlinear, Zelda-like exploration in oblique perspective. Myer throws his sword in eight directions and buys gear with ludder coins. Ten hidden dungeons with invisible entrances; the largest has 235 screens. Invisible portals lead to Parallel Zones and secret rooms with better equipment than the shops.

difficulty.reason: You start very weak: one thrown sword at a time, and some enemies take eight or more hits.

entries.title: Death Race
entries.summary: American Game Cartridges' unlicensed 1990 vehicular combat game, a remake of the 1976 arcade Death Race. Drive an armed sports car through eight US cities.
entries.why_it_matters: One of only three AGCI NES releases (with Shockwave and Chiller). Nintendo Player called it a 'spiritual predecessor' of Grand Theft Auto.
entries.gameplay_notes: Your score is the number of kills. Capture one to four flags, then exit. Spend earnings on engine, tires, chassis, guns and missiles. Four difficulty levels, from Rookie to World Class; finishing the game means clearing every city twice on World Class.

entries.title: Defender II
entries.summary: HAL's NES port of Williams' 1981 arcade shooter Stargate, the sequel to Defender, renamed Defender II in the US.
entries.why_it_matters: Stargate was designed by Eugene Jarvis and Larry DeMar; some home ports were renamed Defender II for legal reasons.
entries.gameplay_notes: Fly over a wrap-around landscape protecting humanoids from abduction. Use a rapid beam, limited smart bombs and a limited Inviso cloak that makes the ship invulnerable. A mini-map shows every alien and human. The Stargate warps you to humanoids in trouble.

entries.content_notes: The NES port's music shares cues with HAL-era Millipede, Joust and Punch-Out!!.
review_flags: Gameplay text describes the arcade game; NES-specific differences are not documented. NA date disagreement: Wikipedia says October 1988, the NOA list says July 1988.

entries.title: Defender of the Crown
entries.summary: Ultra Games' NES conversion of Cinemaware's 1986 Amiga strategy game: as one of four Saxon lords in 1149 England, fight the Normans and rival Saxons for the crown.
entries.why_it_matters: The Amiga original set a new standard for home computer graphics; the NES version trades that polish for more in-depth strategy.
entries.gameplay_notes: Raise armies, besiege and loot castles, fight field battles and win territory in jousting tournaments. You can rescue damsels and call on Robin Hood. At heart it is a war of attrition over army size and timing.

entries.content_notes: The source says the NES and DOS versions have weaker graphics and audio than the Amiga original but deeper strategy.

entries.title: Defenders of Dynatron City
entries.summary: Lucasfilm Games' NES-exclusive superhero action game, published by JVC. A team of super-powered misfits protects a futuristic city from Dr. Mayhem and his robots.
entries.why_it_matters: Gary Winnick's first project as sole designer after co-designing Maniac Mansion. It was backed by an animated TV pilot and a six-issue comic.
entries.gameplay_notes: Heroes include Ms. Megawatt (electricity), Jet Headstrong (fires his head like a rocket), Buzzsaw Girl, the robot Toolbox and Monkey Kid (exploding bananas).

difficulty.reason: Critics singled out notoriously poor hit detection that demands very precise attacks.

entries.title: Déjà Vu
entries.summary: Kemco's NES version of ICOM's 1985 MacVenture point-and-click adventure: amnesiac 1940s Chicago detective Ace Harding must clear his name after being framed for murder.
entries.why_it_matters: The first game in ICOM's MacVenture series, themed after hardboiled detective novels and films.
entries.gameplay_notes: Menu-driven point-and-click investigation in a hardboiled detective story. The NES version changes the memory-loss mechanic, giving unlimited time to find a cure, though visiting Ace's office while still amnesiac is instant death.

entries.title: Demon Sword
entries.summary: Tose-developed Taito action platformer in which Victar recovers three pieces of a shattered blade across three worlds to slay a demon.
entries.why_it_matters: Plays much like Taito's earlier The Legend of Kage.
entries.gameplay_notes: Seven stages (two per world, plus a final stage), each ending in a boss. The sword grows longer and stronger as pieces are recovered. Also use darts, power beams and magic. Big jumps with mid-air turns; you can land on and run across treetops. Watch for pits.

entries.title: Desert Commander
entries.summary: Kemco's turn-based WWII strategy game set in North Africa: command Patton's and Montgomery's Allied forces against Rommel across five scenarios.
entries.why_it_matters: Well received by critics, who praised its balance of strategy and action.
entries.gameplay_notes: Win by taking the enemy HQ or wiping out their forces. Nine unit types plus an HQ, each strong or weak against particular foes. Units can't be built, only resupplied at buildings or by supply trucks. Terrain matters. Later maps get harder only because the CPU has more units. Includes a two-player versus mode; controller 2 can edit CPU forces in one-player games.
